newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico will not run big deficits - Zedillo.
newsitem.headline: Mexico will not run big deficits - Zedillo.

text.p: Mexico has no intention of running big budget deficits to boost its economy out of recession, President Ernesto Zedillo told Reuters in an interview on Tuesday.
Zedillo said one of Mexico's biggest economic problems was its lack of internal savings.

This meant, he explained, that his country "would do very badly to have a lax fiscal policy, which would mean a fall in public savings to the detriment of private savings because that would be limiting our future growth possibilities."

Mexico will run a deficit of 0.5 percent of GDP next year but Zedillo ruled out any substantial widening of that gap in subsequent years, saying even large European economies with big deficits were heading for trouble.

"Developed countries which have deficits are fighting to reduce them because it can't be ruled out that those countries will face severe economic crises in very few years for not having resolved their deficit problems," he said.
Zedillo said the solution to Mexico's lack of internal savings was a tax reform raising sales tax -- which has already been implemented -- and the introduction of a private pensions system.
He shrugged off the delay of six months in the start of private pensions next year, which was recently announced by the government.

"It was for a very practical and important reason," Zedillo said. "To start with an absolutely impeccable operating system, of handling and administration of these pension funds. Not to put a foot wrong."

Questioned about news reports that 1997 would be another year of sacrifice for Mexicans still reeling from the blow of the 1994-95 economic crisis, Zedillo said: "fiscal and monetary discipline must prevail".
"It would be demagogic and populist to tell people there is a magic recipe for Mexicans to have the well-being we want and deserve overnight," he said.

"We have to tell people the truth. First we had to face a very serious crisis. We faced it and we overcame it. Now we have the challenge of transforming a recovery into a process of dynamic sustained growth."
Zedillo also denied that a gap between Mexico's richer more developed north and its poorer south was widening.

"Traditionally the north of the country has been more vigorous and I think that is because of its economic link abroad," he said. "Now the whole country has opened up to the world I think our opportunities for development to be more even are greater."

Asked whether his Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI) was ready to hand over power to the opposition if it lost control of the lower house of congress in elections next July, Zedillo replied: "The PRI has shown that it is a party which respects the law...I am sure the elections in 1997 will be legal and clean. What do I hope for ? For the PRI to win."

But he said he would have no problem working with the opposition, should they win, because of Mexico's experience over the past few years in working with opposition governors and mayors up and down the country.
